facts.fact_text: The United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden (also referred to as 'the applicant association' or 'Ilinden') is an association based in south-western Bulgaria.
At the relevant time Mr Boris Stankov was the chairman of a branch of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.

According to the applicants' submissions before the Court, the main activity of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was the organisation of celebrations to commemorate historical events of importance for Macedonians in Bulgaria.
The United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden held a meeting for the first time on 22 April 1990 at the Rozhen Monastery, at the grave of Yane Sandanski.
On 20 April 1991 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden organised a commemoration meeting at the Rozhen Monastery.
According to the 1998 police report, on 20 April 1991 about 300 to 350 Ilinden supporters had gathered during the official commemoration of the death of Yane Sandanski.
According to the 1998 police report, the official commemoration of the death of Yane Sandanski on 20 April 1991 had been attended by 4,000 participants.
Despite the refusal of the authorities, on 31 July 1994 some members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden attempted to approach the historical site of Samuilova krepost.
According to the applicants' assessment, approximately 120 to 150 members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden attempted to approach Samuilova krepost on 31 July 1994.

The applicants submitted that a group of their supporters who had travelled to the Rozhen Monastery on 22 April 1995 had been ordered by the police to leave their cars in the nearby town of Melnik and had been transported to the monastery by local buses.
The applicants submitted that on 22 April 1995 their supporters had been allowed to visit the grave of Yane Sandanski at the Rozhen Monastery, to lay a wreath and to light candles.
The applicants claimed that on 20 April 1997 the police had prevented a group of their supporters from approaching the Rozhen Monastery.
The applicants submitted that on 20 April 1997 only thirteen students and two teachers from the local high school had arrived at the Rozhen Monastery.

The applicants submitted that on 2 August 1997 the police had not allowed a group of supporters of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden to reach the historical site of Samuilova krepost in the vicinity of Petrich.
In 1990 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was refused registration.
On 13 July 1994 the mayor of Petrich refused permission for the meeting requested by Mr Stankov, without giving any reasons.
The Petrich District Court dismissed the appeal on 16 July 1994.

On 28 July 1994 Mr Ivanov, the representative of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden, was issued with a written warning by the police to stay away from the official traditional fair at Samuilova krepost.
On 28 July 1994 another person (in addition to Mr Ivanov) was issued with a written warning by the police to stay away from the official traditional fair at Samuilova krepost.

On 31 July 1994 the police blocked the way of members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden attempting to approach Samuilova krepost; according to the applicants, the police were heavily armed.
On 14 April 1995 the mayor of Sandanski refused the request for a meeting on 22 April 1995, on the ground that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was not duly registered by the courts.
The Sandanski District Court never examined the appeal lodged by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden on 15 April 1995.

The applicants submitted that on 22 April 1995 their supporters had not been allowed to bring placards, banners and musical instruments to the site of the grave of Yane Sandanski at the Rozhen Monastery.
The applicants submitted that on 22 April 1995 their supporters had not been allowed to make speeches at the grave of Yane Sandanski at the Rozhen Monastery.
The applicants submitted that the police had taken away the ribbon attached to the wreath laid by their supporters at the Rozhen Monastery on 22 April 1995.
On 14 July 1995 the mayor of Petrich refused the request for a meeting on 30 July 1995 at Samuilova krepost without giving any reason.
By judgment of 18 July 1995 the Petrich District Court upheld the mayor of Petrich's refusal to authorise the meeting on 30 July 1995 at Samuilova krepost.
On 11 April 1997 the mayor of Sandanski refused to grant permission for the meeting planned for 20 April 1997 at the Rozhen Monastery.

On 17 April 1997 the President of the Sandanski District Court issued an order refusing to examine the appeal on the merits on the ground that it had been submitted on behalf of an unregistered organisation.

As the defects in the appeal of 15 April 1997 were not remedied within the statutory seven-day time-limit, on 5 May 1997 the President of the Sandanski District Court ordered the discontinuance of the proceedings.
The applicants claimed that on 20 April 1997 the police had prevented a group of their supporters from approaching the Rozhen Monastery.

On 17 July 1997 the mayor of Petrich refused the request for a meeting on 2 August 1997 at Samuilova krepost, stating that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was not 'a legitimate organisation'.
By decision of 1 August 1997 the Petrich District Court dismissed the appeal on the merits.

The applicants submitted that on 2 August 1997 the police had not allowed a group of supporters of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden to reach the historical site of Samuilova krepost in the vicinity of Petrich.
The courts found that registration of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden would be contrary to Articles 3, 8 and 52 § 3 of the Bulgarian Constitution of 1971, as in force at the time.

The judgment of the Supreme Court of 11 March 1991 stated that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was directed against the unity of the nation and was therefore prohibited under Article 35 § 3 of the Bulgarian Constitution of 1971.
Article 43 § 1 of the Bulgarian Constitution of July 1991 provides that everyone shall have the right to peaceful and unarmed assembly at meetings and marches.
Article 43 § 2 of the Bulgarian Constitution of July 1991 provides that the procedure for organising and holding meetings and marches shall be provided for by act of Parliament.

Article 44 § 2 of the Bulgarian Constitution of July 1991 prohibits organisations whose activities are directed against the sovereignty or the territorial integrity of the country or against the unity of the nation, or aim at stirring up racial, national, ethnic or religious hatred, or at violating the rights and freedoms of others, as well as organisations creating secret or paramilitary structures, or which seek to achieve their aims through violence.
The legal requirements for the organisation of meetings are set out in the Bulgarian Meetings and Marches Act of 1990.

Section 8(1) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that where a meeting is to be held outdoors the organisers shall notify in writing the respective People's Council or mayor's office not later than forty-eight hours before the beginning of the meeting, indicating the name of the organiser, the aim of the meeting, and the place and time of the meeting.

Section 12(2) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the President of the Executive Committee of the People's Council or the mayor shall be competent to prohibit the holding of a meeting, demonstration or march where reliable information exists that it aims at the violent overturning of constitutional public order or is directed against the territorial integrity of the country, would endanger public order in the local community, or would breach the rights and freedoms of others.
Section 12(3) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the prohibition shall be imposed by a written reasoned act not later than twenty-four hours following the notification.

Section 12(4) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that the organiser of the meeting, demonstration or march may appeal to the Executive Committee of the People's Council against the prohibition, and the Executive Committee shall decide within twenty-four hours.

Section 12(5) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that where the Executive Committee of the People's Council has not decided within the twenty-four hour time-limit, the march, demonstration or meeting may proceed.

Section 12(6) of the Meetings and Marches Act of 1990 provides that if the appeal is dismissed the dispute shall be referred to the relevant district court which shall decide within five days, and that court's decision shall be final.

The Meetings and Marches Act was adopted in 1990 when the Bulgarian Constitution of 1971 was in force, under which the executive local State organs were the executive committees of the people's councils in each district.

Under the Bulgarian Constitution of 1971, the mayors referred to in some provisions of the Meetings and Marches Act were representatives of the executive committee acting in villages and towns under the jurisdiction of the respective people's councils.

The Bulgarian Constitution of 1991 abolished the executive committees and established the post of mayor, elected by direct universal suffrage, as the 'organ of the executive power in the municipality' under Article 139.
In decisions of July and November 1990 and March 1991, the courts found that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden's aims were directed against the unity of the nation.
In decisions of July and November 1990 and March 1991, the courts found that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden advocated national and ethnic hatred.
In decisions of July and November 1990 and March 1991, the courts found that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was dangerous for the territorial integrity of Bulgaria.

The courts found that the formal declaration in the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden's statute that it would not infringe the territorial integrity of Bulgaria appeared inconsistent with the remaining material.

The judgment of the Supreme Court of 11 March 1991 stated that the lower courts correctly established that the aims of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden under its statute and programme were directed against the unity of the nation.

The judgment of the Supreme Court of 11 March 1991 stated that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden sought to disseminate the ideas of Macedonianism among the Bulgarian population, especially in a particular geographical area.

The judgment of the Supreme Court of 11 March 1991 stated that the ideas of Macedonianism presupposed the 'denationalisation' of the Bulgarian population and its conversion into a Macedonian population.

The judgment of the Supreme Court of 11 March 1991 stated that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was directed against the unity of the nation and was therefore prohibited under Article 35 § 3 of the Bulgarian Constitution of 1971.
According to the 1998 police report, 'fierce anti-Bulgarian declarations' had been made at the meetings of 22 April 1990 and 20 April 1991.

According to the 1998 police report, members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden, standing on a separate platform on 20 April 1991, had allegedly hissed and booed the police, labelled the Bulgarians 'barbarians', 'conquerors' and 'enslavers' and called on them to leave and 'free' the region from their presence.
According to the 1998 police report, a 'shocking' incident had occurred on 20 April 1991 in which Mr B., a prominent politician, had been splashed with beer on his face.
The 1998 police report concluded that the events organised by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden were provocative and that there was a real risk of incidents.

The Petrich District Court found that since the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden had been banned, there were well-founded fears that the demonstration would endanger public order and the rights and freedoms of others.
The Petrich District Court found that 'the holding of a commemorative meeting of Ilinden on 30 July 1995 at Samuilova krepost would endanger public order'.
By decision of 1 August 1997 the Petrich District Court dismissed the appeal on the merits.
The Petrich District Court concluded that the lack of clarity as regards the organisers of a public event endangered public order and the rights and freedoms of others.
The Government relied on the declaration of 20 April 1991 adopted at the Rozhen Monastery meeting and on the 1998 police report concerning the meetings of 1990 and 1991.

The Government submitted that during meetings, in letters to institutions or in statements to the media, persons associated with the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden and its supporters had made declarations to the effect that they wanted the Bulgarians to leave the region of Pirin Macedonia.

The Government submitted that persons associated with the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden and its supporters had stated that there could be 'no peace in the Balkans unless the Bulgarians, the Greeks and all others recognise the national rights of the Macedonian people and no democracy in any Balkan country without such recognition'.

Before the Court the Government relied on a judgment of the Bulgarian Constitutional Court of 29 February 2000 in a case concerning the constitutionality of a political party called the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden-PIRIN: Party for Economic Development and Integration of the Population (UMOIPIRIN), which had been registered by the competent courts in 1999.

The Bulgarian Constitutional Court found in its judgment of 29 February 2000 that the aims of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden-PIRIN: Party for Economic Development and Integration of the Population (UMOIPIRIN) were directed against the territorial integrity of the country and that therefore it was unconstitutional.
The Bulgarian Constitutional Court observed that there had been repeated calls by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden for autonomy and even secession.
The Bulgarian Constitutional Court noted that representatives of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden had made offensive remarks about the Bulgarian nation.

The Bulgarian Constitutional Court found that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden and UMOIPIRIN considered the region of Pirin as a territory which was only temporarily under Bulgarian control and would soon become independent.

The Bulgarian Constitutional Court found that the activities of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden and UMOIPIRIN were directed against the territorial integrity of the country and were prohibited under Article 44 § 2 of the Bulgarian Constitution of 1991.

The Bulgarian Constitutional Court found that the prohibition was in conformity with Article 11 § 2 of the Convention, there being no doubt that an activity against the territorial integrity of the country endangered its national security.
In support of the allegation that some members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden were in possession of arms, the Government submitted copies of two documents.
The first document submitted by the Government was a copy of an article from the Kontinent daily newspaper, dated 1/2 March 1997.

The Kontinent daily newspaper article of 1/2 March 1997 stated that a Mr D.P.K. had been arrested in Petrich for having threatened police officers with blowing up their homes, as they had impeded his business.
According to the Kontinent daily newspaper article of 1/2 March 1997, during the arrest of Mr D.P.K. the police had allegedly discovered explosives in his home.
The Kontinent daily newspaper article of 1/2 March 1997 recalled that Mr D.P.K. was allegedly a leader of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden and a 'Macedonian activist'.
The flyer stated that the United Macedonian Organisation Nova would form armed groups with the aim of 'helping the Republic of Macedonia to survive'.
Section 8 of the statute of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden stated that the organisation would not infringe the territorial integrity of Bulgaria.
Section 9 of the statute of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden stated that the organisation 'would not use violent, brutal, inhuman or unlawful means'.
At the commemoration meeting of 20 April 1991 at the Rozhen Monastery, the participants adopted a declaration addressed to the President and Parliament of Bulgaria.

The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded that minority rights, of which the participants stated they had been deprived, should be guaranteed in accordance with international agreements on minorities.
The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded the introduction of the study of the Macedonian language, history and culture in all educational institutions in Pirin Macedonia.
The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded the right to radio and television broadcasts in the Macedonian language.
The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded that an end be put to the assimilation process and the destruction of the Macedonian culture.
The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded the right to publish in the Macedonian language.
The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded that the Macedonian Church should be independent.

The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded that all Bulgarian political parties on the territory of Pirin Macedonia should be dissolved or renamed Macedonian and should defend the national rights of the Macedonian people.

The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 demanded the complete cultural, economic and political autonomy of Pirin Macedonia and the withdrawal of the Bulgarian occupation armies from Pirin Macedonia.

The declaration adopted at the meeting of 20 April 1991 stated that should the Bulgarian government not respond positively to the demands, Ilinden would appeal to the United Nations Organisation, the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, the European Parliament and the Great Powers, demanding annulment of the separatist military union of 20 February 1912 between Bulgaria, Serbia and Greece, withdrawal of the invaders from the occupied territories, and unification of Macedonia under the auspices of the United Nations and with the protection of the Great Powers.
According to the 1998 police report, on 22 April 1990 a declaration requesting the recognition of a Macedonian minority and cultural autonomy had been read out.
The 1998 police report did not mention any incident at the meeting of 22 April 1990.
According to the 1998 police report, the police had allegedly prevented any further clashes at the meeting of 20 April 1991.
The 1998 police report stated that since 1992 the municipalities in the region had normally refused to allow events organised by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden to proceed.

The 1998 police report stated that with a view to protecting the law, the assistance of the prosecuting authorities and of the police was normally sought in relation to events organised by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.

The applicants submitted copies of photographs, written testimonies and statements of persons who claimed that on several occasions between 1990 and 1994 there had been police actions obstructing the activities of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.

The applicants submitted copies of photographs, written testimonies and statements of persons who claimed that on several occasions between 1990 and 1994 there had been acts of private individuals obstructing the activities of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.
The applicants submitted copies of newspaper articles accusing the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden of misappropriating Bulgarian national symbols.
The applicants submitted copies of newspaper articles describing the leaders of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden as uneducated, mentally ill or traitors.
The applicants submitted copies of newspaper articles denying the existence of a Macedonian minority in Bulgaria.
The applicants alleged that the newspaper articles reflected public opinion in Bulgaria as manipulated by the authorities.
The Government submitted that the allegation that the area of Samuilova krepost had been sealed off on 31 July 1994 was 'manifestly ill-founded'.
The applicants submitted that on 22 April 1995 the participants celebrated the event without music, near the Rozhen Monastery but away from the grave.

In a letter to the mayor of Sandanski, the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden stated that Yane Sandanski, who is considered in Bulgaria as a Bulgarian national hero, was in fact a 'Macedonian fighter for the national independence of Macedonia from Turkish rule and against the Bulgarian oppressors'.
The mayor of Sandanski stated that permission for the commemoration of the same historical event had been requested on 4 April 1997 by the director of the local high school.
The mayor of Sandanski explained that the commemoration on 20 April 1997 would be organised jointly by the local high school and the municipality and that 'every [person], individually, could come'.

On 15 April 1997 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden appealed to the Sandanski District Court against the mayor of Sandanski's refusal of 11 April 1997, stating inter alia that the mayor had not allowed them, 'as a separate ethnic community', to organise a meeting at the tomb of their national hero.
The applicants initially denied having received a response to their appeal of 15 April 1997.
In later submissions to the Commission, the applicants stated that on 5 May 1997 they had become aware of the order of 17 April 1997 issued by the President of the Sandanski District Court.
The order of 5 May 1997 discontinuing the proceedings was notified to the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden on 13 August 1997.
The applicants claimed that on 20 April 1997 two persons had been ill-treated by the police.
The applicants submitted that on 20 April 1997 the students had laid a wreath at the Rozhen Monastery in the presence of the police and had left two minutes later.

On 20 July 1997 the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden appealed to the Petrich District Court against the mayor of Petrich's refusal of 17 July 1997, stating inter alia that there was no legal provision prohibiting meetings of organisations which were not 'legitimate' and that the planned public event would be peaceful and would not endanger public order.
The Petrich District Court found that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden was not duly registered 'in accordance with the laws of the country'.
The Petrich District Court found that it had not been shown that the persons who had acted on behalf of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden actually represented it.
The parties made submissions and presented copies of documents concerning the activities of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.

Some of the documents relied upon by the Government appear to concern statements of persons adhering to a faction or a branch of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden, which groups apparently differed in their views and activities.

The Government submitted copies of several issues of Vestnik za Makedonzite v Balgaria i Po Sveta and Makedonska poshta, pamphlets published by one of the factions linked to the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.
The Government submitted copies of press material relating to the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden and factions linked to it.
The submitted material contained information about a 'secret' private meeting of a faction of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden held on 28 September 1997.

The meeting of 28 September 1997 allegedly declared that on 10 August 1998 the region of Pirin Macedonia would become 'politically, economically and culturally autonomous' or independent, on the basis that eighty-five years after the Bucharest Treaty of 1913 the States Parties to it were allegedly under obligation to withdraw from the 'enslaved' Macedonian territories.
Makedonska poshta invited all Macedonians to a march in Sofia on 3 August 1998, stressing that the participants should not carry arms.

A handwritten poster, allegedly issued by followers of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden in Petrich, called for a boycott of the 1994 parliamentary election 'to prevent the establishment of legitimate Bulgarian authorities in the region' of Pirin Macedonia.
The handwritten poster allegedly issued by followers of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden in Petrich called for a united Macedonian State.

The handwritten poster allegedly issued by followers of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden in Petrich called for 'an international invasion' by the Security Council of the United Nations 'according to the model of Grenada, Kuwait and Haiti'.
An appeal for a boycott of the 1997 election stated that the Macedonians should abstain from voting in protest against the lack of recognition of their rights as a minority.

In a declaration published in the press in the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, the leaders of a faction linked to the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden criticised the Bulgarian authorities for their refusal to recognise the Macedonian language and the Macedonian minority in Bulgaria.

In a declaration published in the press in the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, the leaders of a faction linked to the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden appealed to various international organisations to exert pressure on the Bulgarian authorities to recognise the Macedonian language and the Macedonian minority in Bulgaria.
The Government submitted a copy of a 'memorandum' addressed to the United Nations, signed by activists of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden or a faction of it, dated 1 July 1997.
The memorandum of 1 July 1997 contained a short overview of historical events and complaints about the attitude of the Bulgarian authorities.

The memorandum of 1 July 1997 demanded collective minority rights, access to Bulgarian State archives, the return of confiscated material, the revision of the way Bulgarian history is seen, the revision of international treaties of 1912 and 1913, the dissolution of the 'political police', the dissolution of nationalistic and violent parties and organisations, the registration of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden as the legitimate organisation of the Macedonians in Bulgaria, radio broadcasts in Macedonian, an investigation into violations committed against Macedonians and economic assistance.

The memorandum of 1 July 1997 stated that the signatories were not acting through confrontation, tension or violence, and that their way to achieve enjoyment of their rights as a Macedonian ethnic minority in Bulgaria and in Pirin Macedonia was through peaceful means and negotiations.

The memorandum of 1 July 1997 stated that the signatories' peaceful and lawful means were to the advantage of the authorities who denied the existence of a Macedonian minority, and that the authorities could afford political, economic and psychological pressure, and arms.

The Bulgarian Constitutional Court noted that the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden-PIRIN: Party for Economic Development and Integration of the Population (UMOIPIRIN) could be regarded as a successor to or a continuation of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.

On that basis the Bulgarian Constitutional Court relied extensively on submissions about the history and the activities of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden in the assessment of the question whether UMOIPIRIN was constitutional.
The Bulgarian Constitutional Court took note of the demands made in the declaration of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden of 20 April 1991 adopted at the Rozhen Monastery.
The Bulgarian Constitutional Court observed that maps of the region depicting parts of Bulgarian and Greek territory as Macedonian had been published by the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.
The Bulgarian Constitutional Court's judgment of 29 February 2000 was adopted by nine votes to three.
The dissenting judges in the Bulgarian Constitutional Court's judgment of 29 February 2000 gave separate opinions which have not been published.

The Government did not provide any comment or additional information on the contents of the two documents submitted by them in support of the allegation that some members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden were in possession of arms.

During the hearing before the Court, the Government's Agent declared that no criminal proceedings relevant to the present case had ever been brought against members of the United Macedonian Organisation Ilinden.
The Government stressed that knowledge of the historical context and of the current situation in Bulgaria and in the Balkans was essential for the understanding of the issues in the present case.
According to the Government's historical summary, the Bulgarian nation consolidated within several geographical regions, one of them being the geographical region of Macedonia.

According to the Government's historical summary, in 1878, when Bulgaria was partially liberated from Turkish dominance, the Berlin Peace Treaty left the region of Macedonia within the borders of Turkey.

According to the Government's historical summary, between 1878 and 1913 the Bulgarian population of Macedonia organised five unsuccessful uprisings seeking liberation from Turkish rule and union with Bulgaria, followed by massive refugee migrations from the region to Bulgaria, with hundreds of thousands of Macedonian Bulgarians settling in Bulgaria.

According to the Government's historical summary, in 1934 the so-called 'Macedonian nation' was proclaimed for the first time by a resolution of the Communist International, and before that no reliable historical source had ever mentioned any Slavic population in the region other than the Bulgarian population.

According to the Government's historical summary, after the Second World War the Communist power in Yugoslavia proclaimed the concept of a separate Macedonian nation, and a separate language and alphabet were created and imposed by decree of 2 August 1944.
According to the Government's historical summary, a massive assimilation campaign accompanied by brutalities was launched in Yugoslavia following the proclamation of a separate Macedonian nation.

According to the Government's historical summary, for a short period the Bulgarian Communist Party, inspired by the idea of creating a Bulgarian-Yugoslav federation, initiated a campaign of forcible imposition of a 'Macedonian' identity on the population in the region of Pirin Macedonia, and in the 1946 and 1956 censuses individuals living in that region were forced to declare themselves 'Macedonians'; the campaign was abandoned in 1963, partly due to the refusal of the population to change their identity.
According to the Government's historical summary, even if a process of formation of a new nation took place, it was limited to the territory of the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.
According to the Government's historical summary, in the 1992 census only 3,019 Bulgarian citizens identified themselves as Macedonians and indicated Macedonian as their mother tongue.

According to the Government's historical summary, in the 1992 census another 7,784 Bulgarian citizens declared themselves Macedonians in the geographical sense, while allegedly indicating their Bulgarian national conscience and mother tongue.

According to the Government's historical summary, individuals considering themselves Macedonians are not discriminated against in Bulgaria, have their own cultural and educational organisation called Svetlina, and there are books and newspapers in the 'Macedonian language'.
